info.desc: Unknown Pleasures is the debut studio album by English rock band Joy Division, released on 15 June 1979 on Tony Wilson's Factory Records. It followed an abandoned session for RCA Records, and was recorded and mixed over three weekends at Strawberry Studios, Stockport in April 1979 with record producer Martin Hannett. The cover artwork was designed by artist Peter Saville. Factory did not release any singles from the album, and it did not chart despite the relative success of the group's non-album debut single "Transmission". Unknown Pleasures has gone on to receive sustained critical acclaim as a pioneering and influential .

podcast.body: Recorded in April 1979 at Strawberry Studios with producer Martin Hannett, this album, financed by Tony Wilson for 8,500 pounds for 10,000 copies, was hailed by reviews as the "most radical post-punk record of the year" and a "masterpiece," immediately selling out its first pressing. Its distinctive sound was achieved by Hannett's innovative production techniques, including recording drums on the studio roof and employing "cold intimacy." "The name of the album was unknown pleasures. Joy Division and Disorder, for unknown pleasures, one of the most important post-punk alternative records of all time."

podcast.body: The packaging, designed by Peter Saville, is entirely black except for a white illustration resembling a mountain range. This image is actually a visual representation of 100 consecutive pulses from a pulsar named CP1919 in the constellation Vulpecula, sourced from "The Cambridge Encyclopedia of Astronomy." The cover has become immensely popular, launching a million t-shirts, posters, and imitations, including a Disney co-opted Mickey Mouse t-shirt in 2012. "The whole thing was black, save for what looked like a white illustration of a mountain range. podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: The recording of Joy Division's first album, *Unknown Pleasures*, began in 1979. It is considered a possible peak work of Post-Punk and a key origin point for the genre. The pure recording process was very fast, taking only three to five weekends, but the overall production was protracted because the band members had day jobs and could only record on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays. The band entered the recording sessions with a clear idea and polished vision for the songs, having already developed a detailed demo and experienced a failed recording contract with RCA. The album was released several months after its recording. It achieved relative success, selling well for an independent, almost self-produced album, though it was not a major chart hit and didn't reach the top 70s. Its success enabled the band to tour extensively and become full-time professional musicians. Despite its current critical acclaim, *Unknown Pleasures* was not widely reviewed at the time of its release, and many contemporary "reviews" found today are retrospective, often from the late 1990s or 2000s. The album's legacy is that it significantly influenced many bands, like The Cure, who in turn influenced the public, rather than directly influencing the general public itself, drawing a comparison to The Velvet Underground's debut. "Continuamos este pequeño especial sobre la vida y la carrera de J-Division en el punto en el que lo habíamos dejado el momento anterior, que es justo 1979 cuando comienza la grabación de No Pleasure's, el primer disco del J-Division."
